title: Is Nextel Still Around in 2026? Chirp Died in 2013
body:
Nextel is not around in 2026. Sprint began shutting down the iDEN network that carried Nextel Direct Connect at 12:01 a.m. Eastern on June 30, 2013, and no US carrier has sold a Nextel-branded plan since. The name itself belongs to Sprint Communications, now part of T-Mobile, which beat back an attempt to claim the brand as abandoned when the Eleventh Circuit affirmed its trademark win on April 4, 2024.

Quick facts
What it was
Push-to-talk carrier on Motorola's iDEN network
Bought by Sprint
August 2005, reported at $35 billion
Written off
$29.6 billion goodwill impairment for 2007
Status today
Gone; iDEN shutdown began 12:01 a.m. Eastern, June 30, 2013
Owner today
Sprint Communications, part of T-Mobile; marks upheld in 2024

Why contractors paid extra for a phone that chirped

Nextel was never a conventional cellular carrier. It ran on the 800 MHz specialized mobile radio band, the dispatch spectrum the Federal Communications Commission had set aside for fleet use, and on iDEN, a system Motorola built to pack several users onto a single radio channel.

That tradeoff made iDEN efficient for short dispatch bursts and mediocre for long phone calls. Nextel sold a two-way radio that happened to be a phone, to customers who had always carried radios, while every other carrier sold phones to everyone else.

Nextel Direct Connect was the reason to buy one. Press the button on the side of the handset, hear the two-tone chirp, and you were talking to a co-worker or a whole crew without dialing a number or waiting for a ring.

By the end of July 2003, Nextel and its regional affiliate Nextel Partners had finished rolling out Nationwide Direct Connect across the continental United States and Hawaii, which put more than 14 million Nextel and Nextel Partners subscribers within reach of the button.

Nextel Partners told the Securities and Exchange Commission in its 2003 annual report that the feature "has been responsible for our strong appeal to business users in mobile occupations," and named transportation, delivery, facilities management, construction and building, and landscaping as the industries it came from.

What Sprint paid for Nextel, and what it wrote off

Sprint closed its acquisition of Nextel Communications in August 2005 at a price RCR Wireless reported as $35 billion. The combined company counted about 44 million customers once network partners were included, which put it third in the US market behind Verizon and Cingular.

It also had two incompatible networks: Sprint's CDMA system and Nextel's iDEN. Moving a customer from one to the other meant selling them a new phone, and push-to-talk on CDMA did not behave the way iDEN users expected it to.

The accounting caught up in 2007. Sprint Nextel's annual report for 2008 records non-cash goodwill impairment charges of $963 million for 2008 and $29.6 billion for 2007, and states that those charges "relate solely to the Wireless segment."

After the 2008 assessment, the same filing says, no goodwill remained on the consolidated balance sheet at all. Sprint had written off most of what it paid for Nextel within roughly two years of buying it, and the brand was already shedding the business users it had been bought for.

What happened at 12:01 a.m. on June 30, 2013

Sprint announced the shutdown more than a year ahead of time and confirmed the schedule in June 2013. Decommissioning began at 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sunday, June 30, 2013, and worked westward by time zone, hour by hour.

After that moment, Sprint said, iDEN devices would no longer receive voice service, including 911 calls, push-to-talk or data. There was no grace period and no roaming agreement to fall back on, because no other US carrier ran iDEN.

Bob Azzi, Sprint's senior vice president of network, had spent the previous year pushing customers off the system. "We strongly urge customers to migrate now to the Sprint Nationwide CDMA network to avoid losing service," he said in the company's June 2013 announcement.

The destination was Sprint Direct Connect, a push-to-talk service on CDMA that Sprint said covered three times the push-to-talk area iDEN had. Plenty of crews treated the shutdown as a reason to change carriers instead. The spectrum was the real prize: once iDEN went dark, Sprint refarmed its 800 MHz holdings for LTE.

Who owns the Nextel name in 2026?

No carrier sells a Nextel-branded plan in the United States, and nothing has carried the name on a US network since June 30, 2013. The trademarks did not go anywhere, though. They stayed with Sprint Communications, which is now part of T-Mobile, which is why the word turns up in trademark paperwork and nowhere on a store shelf.

That ownership was tested in court. Retrobrands USA and Nextel Mobile Worldwide sold phones under the Nextel name and promoted a revival of the brand, arguing that it had been abandoned, since US trademark law treats three consecutive years of nonuse as prima facie evidence of abandonment.

Sprint sued for infringement, counterfeiting and cybersquatting. A Florida jury found that Sprint had not abandoned either the Nextel word mark or the chirp sound mark and awarded $4.5 million in statutory damages, and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed that judgment on April 4, 2024, in Sprint Communications LLC v. Retrobrands USA, LLC.

So the answer to the question people type is that T-Mobile holds Nextel through Sprint Communications, and that it has defended the name hard enough to stop anyone else from relighting it as a carrier.

Can a Nextel phone do anything in 2026?

A Motorola iDEN handset from 2006 will still power on if the battery holds a charge, show its menu, and find no signal anywhere. The only network it could speak to stopped existing in 2013, and nothing replaced it on the same air interface, so there is no carrier to unlock it to and no SIM swap that helps.

That makes a Nextel phone a display object rather than a spare. The chirp has had the stranger afterlife of the two: it is still a registered sound mark that a federal appeals court has ruled on, which is more than can be said for the handsets.

Other hardware from those years landed differently. Pagers are still in daily use in US hospitals because the networks behind them were never switched off, and the Motorola Razr V3 has a more complicated answer, because parts of the world it was built for survive and parts do not.

What replaced Direct Connect on today's phones

Push-to-talk did not die with iDEN. It moved into software. Sprint Direct Connect ran on CDMA until T-Mobile retired the Sprint CDMA network after the merger, and the function now travels as data over LTE and 5G instead of riding a band of its own.

Zello turns an ordinary phone into a channel-based radio over Wi-Fi or cellular data. Motorola Solutions sells WAVE PTX, which bridges broadband phones with the land mobile radio systems police forces and utility crews still operate. AT&T sells Enhanced Push-to-Talk to business customers, and Verizon offers a comparable service.

What none of them rebuilt is the thing Nextel customers were actually buying: one carrier where the button behaved identically for everyone on the account, on hardware designed around it, with a tone every tradesperson recognized across a parking lot. An app depends on a data connection, a login and a battery doing more work.

Nextel's buyers were the same business users the BlackBerry chased later in the decade, and both brands learned the same lesson: the feature that defines a company can be copied into software by everyone else.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Nextel still around in 2026?

No. Nextel has not run a network in the United States since Sprint began decommissioning the iDEN system at 12:01 a.m. Eastern on June 30, 2013, and no carrier has sold a Nextel-branded plan in the US since. The Nextel trademarks sit with Sprint Communications, now part of T-Mobile, so the name survives on paper rather than on a network.

Who owns the Nextel brand now?

Sprint Communications, a T-Mobile company, owns the Nextel word mark and the Nextel chirp sound mark. After Retrobrands USA and Nextel Mobile Worldwide tried to revive the brand on the argument that it had been abandoned, a Florida jury found Sprint had not abandoned either mark and awarded $4.5 million in statutory damages, and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed that judgment on April 4, 2024.

Can you still use a Nextel phone?

Not as a phone. The Motorola iDEN handsets Nextel sold through June 2013 worked only on the iDEN network, which has been switched off since June 30, 2013, and no other US carrier uses iDEN, so they cannot be reactivated or moved to another network. A Nextel handset in 2026 powers on, shows its menu and finds no service.
